extracted.intended_audience: general readers; fans of animated television; writers/researchers interested in TV comedy production
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts the creative and production criteria, comedic techniques, and storytelling standards used in the animated sitcom American Dad! that inform how its humor is produced and judged. Useful for writers, critics, and researchers studying animated comedy style and production practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor derived from characters and relationships (not cutaway gags)
rubrics_metrics.description: American Dad! "does not lean as heavily on the use of cutaway gags, instead deriving its humor mostly from the quirky characters and their relationships."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with Family Guy's reference/cutaway approach; favors situational and character-based comedy. Example: long-running character-driven arcs and Roger's alter egos provide much of the show's humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evergreen / timeless writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers aim to make scripts "timeless, as opposed to topical and contemporary."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid over-reliance on fleeting current events so jokes remain funny years later; if contemporary material is used, hope it will still be relevant two years on. Example: writers had to Google a now-obscure reference (Harriet Miers) when an old joke aired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy from human condition and emotions rather than references
rubrics_metrics.description: Barker described the show's humor as "more frequently deriv[ing] from 'the human condition and emotions that everyone can relate to: ego, the feds, etc.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer emotional and situational cores (ego, family dynamics, institutions) over dense pop-culture or topical references; described as more 'evergreen' and less reference-laden than some peers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Farce through escalation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of farce where predicaments escalate 'to the extremes, to the point of getting outrageously out of hand.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plotlines ramp up consequences and absurdity (examples: dividing the house in 'Home Wrecker'; blowing up a restaurant in 'Stan's Food Restaurant') to generate comedic payoff via escalation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surrealism and nonsensical elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Plots are "generally teeming with surrealism and nonsensical elements," featuring unrestrainedly preposterous, senseless, and illogical occurrences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequent use of bizarre visuals, implausible set-pieces, and logic-defying scenarios (examples: transformable hallways, underground control rooms, animals behaving humanlike) to produce comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non sequitur / story-within-a-story technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent sidetracking into unrelated characters and stories (non sequitur/story within a story), where focus is lost to irrelevant or new characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use brief, seemingly unrelated vignettes (e.g., 'The Golden Turd' storyline) that may continue across episodes; these can act as recurring mini-arcs or running jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot twists and unexpected elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Abundant use of random, unexpected occurrences and surprise plot twists as a core comedic device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce curveballs (e.g., hiring a bully to bully the protagonist, fake vacations revealed as 'goo chambers') that subvert audience expectations for laughs and story momentum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story arcs and continuity (avoid 'reset button')
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of story arcs across multiple episodes and an explicit effort to "obey basic rules of continuity" so big changes persist rather than being quickly reset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow significant events (marriages, character changes, long absences) to have lasting consequences, which increases emotional weight and payoff in later episodes (examples: Jeff's disappearance and return, multi-season Santa arc).

rubrics_metrics.name: Black comedy / edgy subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent use of black comedy — making fun of life-threatening, disastrous, terrifying, or traumatic situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tackle dark themes (suicide, murder, extreme violence) for shock and dark-humor payoff (examples: 'A Ward Show', 'Da Flippity Flop'); combine laughs with groans and intentionally 'go over the line' at times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Running gags and alter egos (character-based comedic devices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of running gags and recurring character devices (notably Roger's many alternate disguises) to provide material and variety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single character can function as multiple 'guest stars' via alter egos, supplying fresh conflict and comedic situations each episode while maintaining continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character evolution and avoiding stagnant dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: Creators learned early that dynamics like constant political banter had a 'limited shelf life' and adjusted characterization accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt characters and relationships over time to avoid repetitive comedic beats; broaden comedic sources beyond an initial conceit (e.g., move beyond pure conservative-vs-liberal banter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Story-breaking group process to craft strong acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot development involves spending weeks in a room with all the screenwriters to break stories and ensure each act and act break is strong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collective story-breaking identifies twists and pacing that will 'make audiences come back for more after the commercial break'; emphasis on structural strength before individual scripts are written.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-week script draft, iterative edits, and table read
rubrics_metrics.description: A screenwriter gets two weeks to write a script which is then edited and rewritten by the team, "punching the jokes and making sure all the motivations are there," followed by a table read.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve as much of the first draft as possible while refining jokes and character motivations in multiple passes; use table reads to test comedic beats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing, completion, and finalization workflow
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of animation, the team can redraw and rewrite until airing, but must ultimately 'bring down the hammer at the color stage' and accept a final version.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance benefit of late-stage changes against sunk time/cost; producers (not external parties) decide when an episode is complete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Animation production standards (preproduction, overseas coloring, storyboards)
rubrics_metrics.description: Much is done in-house (poses, models, props, all storyboards and timing) with coloring and detailing overseas (Yearim Productions, Korea). 'Fifty or so animators from the Fox animation group are involved.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat each episode like a 'little movie' — intricate storyboards, timing, and orchestral scoring; coordinate in-house preproduction with overseas finishing for consistent quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voice acting method: actors record lines privately
rubrics_metrics.description: Voice actors 'are not assembled as a group' when performing lines; each records privately because group sessions would lead to goofing off.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record individually to maintain efficiency and control, relying on direction and editing to assemble performances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of music as a creative muse
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers sometimes use music to inspire plot ideas and tone (Mike Barker credited music from Wax Fang for inspiration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage music's cinematic and lyrical qualities to seed story concepts or to shape episode mood and structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain production buffer of unaired episodes
rubrics_metrics.description: Creators work significantly in advance; as many as '20 to 42 unaired episodes are typically ready for finishing touches.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A production buffer allows time for polishing, safeguards against topicality issues, and supports scheduling flexibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Showrunner/creator control over creative decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: As creative directors, Barker and Weitzman stated that all decisions about plot line and direction go through them; 'the show had reflected their point of view since the beginning.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Centralized creative leadership ensures a coherent tone and vision across episodes and seasons.
